title: Haxtun Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Haxtun wells have a 240-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $14,400-$25,200.
h1: Haxtun, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Buying land around Haxtun means looking closely at the local well record, not relying on a statewide average. Within the mapped area, Colorado Division of Water Resources records show wells commonly completed in the plains sediments and fractured-bedrock formations beneath Phillips County.

The records give a useful starting point for estimating depth, production, water level, and drilling cost. They do not guarantee what a new hole will find on a particular parcel. A driller still needs to review the lot, nearby completions, access, casing and grout requirements, and the intended household or agricultural use.

sections.heading: Haxtun well depths and the formations below town
sections.html:
The median reported well depth around Haxtun is 240 feet. The middle half runs from 206 to 290 feet, and 90% of reported depths are at or below 320 feet. The deepest record reaches 355 feet.

Most wells are not shallow. 77% fall between 100 and 300 feet, while 23% are between 300 and 600 feet. None of the records are under 100 feet or above 600 feet. Permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer on 206 wells and the Ogallala on 98. That mix matters for bidding: use the local depth range as a planning allowance, but do not treat 240 feet as a guaranteed completion depth.

sections.heading: How much water Haxtun wells produce
sections.html:
Reported production is solid in the local records, with a median pump yield of 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 10.0 to 30.0 gallons per minute. Among the wells that report yield, 63% produce more than 15 gallons per minute, 29% fall between 5 and 15, and 8% fall between 1 and 5.

No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute, but the yield sample includes only 52 wells, so it is not a promise for an untested lot. A buyer should ask for the completion report and pumping test, then compare the result with household demand, livestock plans, irrigation, and storage. An exempt household-use well is generally limited to 35 gallons per minute under Colorado rules, subject to the permit terms.

sections.heading: Water levels around Haxtun and what the records show
sections.html:
Only 23 local records report a static water level, so the water-level dataset is much smaller than the depth dataset. Those records show a median depth to static water of 148 feet, with the middle half from 140 to 158 feet.

The available facts do not provide a water-level series by decade, so they do not support a conclusion that the water table is dropping or recovering over time. A static level is also not the same as the water level while pumping. Before buying, obtain the well construction and pump information, check nearby wells in Paoli, Fleming, and the surrounding Phillips County plains, and have a driller evaluate whether the reported water level fits the proposed pump setting and storage system.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Haxtun, and how active is the record
sections.html:
Local permit history stretches from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025. The largest group is from the 1970s, with 56 permits. Other notable decades include the 1990s with 36, the 2000s with 32, and the 2010s with 26.

In the driller records, Wellstone Industries doing business as Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc. and Raymond L. Twiss appear on 30 wells. Stewart Drilling Co. and Dennis W. Stewart appear on 19, while Wellstone Services, LLC and Bryan Beckner appear on 10. These names help when tracing nearby completions, but current availability, licensing, insurance, and site-specific experience still need to be confirmed directly.

sections.heading: What a new Haxtun well may cost
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. A typical drilling rate is $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 240 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $8,400 to $13,200.

That is not the complete project price. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,400 to $25,200 at the same median depth. A bid can move outside that range if the hole must go deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the site needs longer utility runs. Ask for drilling, casing, development, pump, electrical, trenching, testing, and permit-related work to be separated in writing.

sections.heading: Haxtun risks to check before you commit
sections.html:
The main practical risks are low production, an unsuccessful hole, water-quality problems, and costs that appear after drilling. The yield records are encouraging, but only 52 wells report a pump yield. That leaves uncertainty on parcels with no close, comparable completion. A driller should review nearby depths, aquifer names, casing and grout details, and the proposed well location before you buy.

There are 4 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles. There are no recorded historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped search. That does not replace a water test. Test for ordinary drinking-water concerns and any site-specific contaminants, and keep the well separated from septic components. Confirm that the lot has enough room for the well, septic system, reserve area, driveway, and the home site.

sections.heading: Buying or building a lot near Haxtun
sections.html:
Make the well permit and construction report part of the purchase review. Colorado DWR records contain 315 wells in this local dataset, but only 124 are recorded as constructed and 179 report a total depth. Those differences mean a map point or permit count is not the same as a verified producing well.

For a buildable lot, have a licensed driller inspect access and review nearby completions before setting a budget. Confirm the permitted use: local records include domestic or household, stock, and irrigation wells, and the permit controls what the well may legally serve. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, ask the water attorney or permitting professional whether an augmentation plan is needed. Get a septic evaluation, water-quality test, and written drilling allowance before removing inspection contingencies.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Haxtun, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth near Haxtun is 240 feet. The middle half runs from 206 to 290 feet, while the deepest record is 355 feet. Most wells, 77%, are between 100 and 300 feet. Use those figures for planning, not as a guarantee for a specific parcel.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Haxtun?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 240-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $8,400 to $13,200. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $14,400 to $25,200. Access, depth, casing, grout, and utility distance can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a Haxtun well produce?
faq.a: Reported wells have a median pump yield of 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 30.0 gallons per minute. Of 52 wells reporting yield, 63% produce more than 15 gallons per minute. These results are useful local evidence, but a pumping test is still needed for a particular well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Haxtun?
faq.a: The records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. There are 4 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, so a buyer should obtain a laboratory water test and ask about site history. Test the existing well before purchase and retest after major work or if taste, odor, or color changes.

faq.q: Are there enough well records near Haxtun to compare a property?
faq.a: The local dataset contains 315 DWR permit records. Of those, 124 are recorded as constructed, 179 report total depth, and 52 report pump yield. That is enough to identify useful local patterns, but not every map point is a verified producing well. Compare the closest completed wells by depth, aquifer, use, and test results.
